  1. 1

    What is the leading coefficient of 5x2−x4+7−2x5x^{2} - x^{4} + 7 - 2x5x2−x4+7−2x?

    Answer choices for question 1

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose B: Takes the coefficient of the first term written instead of the coefficient of the highest-degree term.

    You chose C: Reports the degree of the polynomial in place of the coefficient attached to its leading term.

    You chose D: Picks out the constant term, the largest number written, rather than the coefficient sitting on the highest power.

    The leading term is the one of highest degree, not the one written first. The degrees present are 222, 444, 000 and 111, so put the polynomial in standard form and read the front of it.

    5x2−x4+7−2x=−x4+5x2−2x+75x^{2} - x^{4} + 7 - 2x = -x^{4} + 5x^{2} - 2x + 75x2−x4+7−2x=−x4+5x2−2x+7

    The leading term is −x4-x^{4}−x4, which is −1x4-1x^{4}−1x4, so the leading coefficient is −1-1−1.

  2. 2

    Which of these rules defines an exponential function?

    Answer choices for question 2

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Sees a variable and a fixed number and calls it exponential, though here the variable is the base and the exponent is frozen, which makes it a power function.

    You chose B: Reads the constant 333 multiplying the variable as a base, though 3x3x3x carries xxx to the first power and is linear.

    You chose D: Checks that the variable is in the exponent but not that the base is allowed, though 1x=11^{x} = 11x=1 for every xxx, which is why the base 111 is excluded.

    A function is exponential when a fixed base carries the variable in its exponent, with that base positive and not equal to 111.

    f(x)=3x:the base 3 is frozen and the exponent x movesf(x) = 3^{x}: \quad \text{the base } 3 \text{ is frozen and the exponent } x \text{ moves}f(x)=3x:the base 3 is frozen and the exponent x moves

    In x3x^{3}x3 the variable sits in the base, so that is a power function, and 3x3x3x is linear. The rule 1x1^{x}1x does put the variable in the exponent, but it collapses to the constant 111.

  3. 3

    Simplify (7x2−2x+5)−(3x2+4x−1)(7x^{2} - 2x + 5) - (3x^{2} + 4x - 1)(7x2−2x+5)−(3x2+4x−1).

    Answer choices for question 3

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Flips the sign of only the first term of the second polynomial, leaving +4x+4x+4x and −1-1−1 as they stand.

    You chose C: Distributes the minus sign to the x2x^{2}x2 and xxx terms but copies the −1-1−1 across unchanged.

    You chose D: Adds the two polynomials instead of subtracting, so every sign inside the second parenthesis survives.

    A minus sign in front of a parenthesis is a factor of −1-1−1 on the whole group, so all three signs inside turn over.

    (7x2−2x+5)−(3x2+4x−1)=7x2−2x+5−3x2−4x+1=4x2−6x+6(7x^{2} - 2x + 5) - (3x^{2} + 4x - 1) = 7x^{2} - 2x + 5 - 3x^{2} - 4x + 1 = 4x^{2} - 6x + 6(7x2−2x+5)−(3x2+4x−1)=7x2−2x+5−3x2−4x+1=4x2−6x+6

    Watch the two signs that changed: the +4x+4x+4x became −4x-4x−4x, and the −1-1−1 became +1+1+1.

    Answer choices for question 4

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Takes log⁡5(1)\log_{5}(1)log5​(1) to be 111, swapping the two standard values log⁡b(1)=0\log_{b}(1) = 0logb​(1)=0 and log⁡b(b)=1\log_{b}(b) = 1logb​(b)=1.

    You chose C: Adds the two inputs 818181 and 111 instead of evaluating each logarithm and adding the results.

    Each logarithm asks for an exponent: what power does the base need? Nine squared is 818181, and any allowed base to the zero power is 111.

    92=81  ⇒  log⁡9(81)=2,50=1  ⇒  log⁡5(1)=09^{2} = 81 \;\Rightarrow\; \log_{9}(81) = 2, \qquad 5^{0} = 1 \;\Rightarrow\; \log_{5}(1) = 092=81⇒log9​(81)=2,50=1⇒log5​(1)=0

  5. 5

    Expand (2x−7)(x+3)(2x - 7)(x + 3)(2x−7)(x+3).

    Answer choices for question 5

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose B: Keeps only the first and the last products and drops the two cross terms.

    You chose C: Loses the minus attached to the 777 in the inner product, so the cross terms add as 6x+7x6x + 7x6x+7x instead of subtracting.

    You chose D: Adds the constants −7-7−7 and 333 where the last product multiplies them.

    Each term of the first binomial multiplies each term of the second, four products in all.

    (2x−7)(x+3)=2x2+6x−7x−21=2x2−x−21(2x - 7)(x + 3) = 2x^{2} + 6x - 7x - 21 = 2x^{2} - x - 21(2x−7)(x+3)=2x2+6x−7x−21=2x2−x−21

    The two middle products are like terms and combine to −x-x−x, and the last product is (−7)(3)=−21(-7)(3) = -21(−7)(3)=−21.

    A savings certificate pays 4%4\%4% compounded annually. On a deposit of 250025002500 dollars, what is the balance after 222 years? Use 1.042=1.08161.04^{2} = 1.08161.042=1.0816.

    Answer choices for question 6

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Uses simple interest, adding 4%4\%4% of the original deposit once for each year instead of multiplying by 1.041.041.04 twice.

    You chose B: Applies the growth factor once, for a single year, rather than once for each of the two years.

    You chose C: Puts the percent 444 into the formula in place of the decimal 0.040.040.04, so each year multiplies the balance by 555.

    The rate is the decimal form of the percent, so r=0.04r = 0.04r=0.04, and annual compounding applies the factor 1+r1 + r1+r once per year.

    A=2500 (1+0.04)2=2500×1.0816=2704A = 2500\,(1 + 0.04)^{2} = 2500 \times 1.0816 = 2704A=2500(1+0.04)2=2500×1.0816=2704

    The balance is 270427042704 dollars. Simple interest would have given 2500(1+0.04×2)=27002500(1 + 0.04 \times 2) = 27002500(1+0.04×2)=2700 dollars, so the extra 444 dollars is interest earned on the first year's interest.

    Which statement describes the graph of f(x)=6⋅(13)xf(x) = 6\cdot\left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)^{x}f(x)=6⋅(31​)x?

    Answer choices for question 7

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Reads every exponential as growth, though a base between 000 and 111 multiplies the output by less than 111 at each step to the right.

    You chose B: Takes the base as the vertical intercept, though the intercept is the value at x=0x = 0x=0, where the power is 111 and only the multiplier survives.

    You chose D: Places the intercept on the wrong axis, though the value at x=0x = 0x=0 is a height and the curve stays above the horizontal axis at every input.

    The base decides the direction. Here it is 13\tfrac{1}{3}31​, which lies between 000 and 111, so each step to the right multiplies the output by 13\tfrac{1}{3}31​ and the graph falls. The intercept is the value at x=0x = 0x=0.

    f(0)=6⋅(13)0=6×1=6f(0) = 6\cdot\left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)^{0} = 6 \times 1 = 6f(0)=6⋅(31​)0=6×1=6

    So the curve falls and meets the vertical axis at 666.

    A function has the form f(x)=a⋅bxf(x) = a\cdot b^{x}f(x)=a⋅bx with a>0a > 0a>0, b>0b > 0b>0 and b≠1b \ne 1b=1. Its outputs at x=0x = 0x=0, x=2x = 2x=2 and x=4x = 4x=4 are 333, 121212 and 484848. What is bbb?

    Answer choices for question 10

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose C: Squares the ratio where the two-unit step calls for a square root, reading b2=4b^{2} = 4b2=4 backwards.

    You chose D: Reports the starting value aaa, the output at x=0x = 0x=0, rather than the base.

    b2=123=4  ⇒  b=2b^{2} = \frac{12}{3} = 4 \;\Rightarrow\; b = 2b2=312​=4⇒b=2

    Then a=3a = 3a=3 from the output at x=0x = 0x=0, and the rule f(x)=3⋅2xf(x) = 3\cdot 2^{x}f(x)=3⋅2x checks out at the far end: 3⋅24=483 \cdot 2^{4} = 483⋅24=48.

    Which expression is the exact solution of 7x=307^{x} = 307x=30? Here log⁡\loglog means the common logarithm, base 101010.

    Answer choices for question 11

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Subtracts the two logarithms where the power law calls for dividing by one of them; that difference is log⁡ ⁣(307)\log\!\left(\tfrac{30}{7}\right)log(730​), a different number.

    You chose B: Writes the quotient upside down, dividing by the logarithm of the number rather than by the logarithm of the base.

    You chose D: Divides the two numbers directly, as though an exponent could be freed without taking a logarithm at all.

    Take the logarithm of both sides, then let the power law bring the exponent down to the ground.

    log⁡ ⁣(7x)=log⁡(30)  ⇒  xlog⁡(7)=log⁡(30)  ⇒  x=log⁡(30)log⁡(7)\log\!\left(7^{x}\right) = \log(30) \;\Rightarrow\; x\log(7) = \log(30) \;\Rightarrow\; x = \frac{\log(30)}{\log(7)}log(7x)=log(30)⇒xlog(7)=log(30)⇒x=log(7)log(30)​

    The last step divides both sides by the number log⁡(7)\log(7)log(7), so the answer is a quotient of two logarithms.

  12. 12

    What are the degree and the leading coefficient of (5x3+2x2−x)−(5x3−4x+7)\left(5x^{3} + 2x^{2} - x\right) - \left(5x^{3} - 4x + 7\right)(5x3+2x2−x)−(5x3−4x+7)?

    Answer choices for question 12

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Takes the degree of a difference to be the larger of the two degrees and copies the 555 from the front, which is exactly what fails when equal leading terms cancel.

    You chose C: Adds the degrees and multiplies the leading coefficients, which is the rule for a product rather than for a difference.

    You chose D: Cancels the 2x22x^{2}2x2 term as well, though the second polynomial has no x2x^{2}x2 term for it to cancel against.

    Distribute the minus sign to all three terms of the second polynomial, then collect.

    5x3+2x2−x−5x3+4x−7=2x2+3x−75x^{3} + 2x^{2} - x - 5x^{3} + 4x - 7 = 2x^{2} + 3x - 75x3+2x2−x−5x3+4x−7=2x2+3x−7

    Both polynomials have degree 333 and the identical leading term 5x35x^{3}5x3, so subtracting wipes that term out and the degree drops to 222. Nothing cancels at x2x^{2}x2, so the leading coefficient of the result is 222.

    A loan of 600060006000 dollars accrues interest at 9%9\%9% compounded quarterly. Which expression gives the amount owed after 555 years?

    Answer choices for question 13

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Divides the rate by 444 but leaves the exponent as the number of years, though the exponent counts periods and there are four of them each year.

    You chose B: Multiplies the exponent by 444 but pays the full yearly rate in every quarter, though each period pays only rn\tfrac{r}{n}nr​.

    You chose C: Uses the percent 999 in place of the decimal 0.090.090.09, so each quarter multiplies the balance by 1+94=3.251 + \tfrac{9}{4} = 3.251+49​=3.25.

    Compounding nnn times a year makes two edits, and both are needed: the rate inside the parentheses is divided by nnn, and the exponent is multiplied by nnn.

    A=6000(1+0.094)4×5=6000 (1.0225)20A = 6000\left(1 + \frac{0.09}{4}\right)^{4 \times 5} = 6000\,(1.0225)^{20}A=6000(1+40.09​)4×5=6000(1.0225)20

    Simplify (x+5)(x−2)−(x−3)2(x + 5)(x - 2) - (x - 3)^{2}(x+5)(x−2)−(x−3)2.

    Answer choices for question 14

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose B: Applies the minus sign to only the first term of the expanded square, leaving its −6x-6x−6x and +9+9+9 with the signs they had.

    You chose C: Flips the sign of the −6x-6x−6x but copies the +9+9+9 across unchanged, so the constant comes out as −10+9-10 + 9−10+9.

    You chose D: Squares x−3x - 3x−3 term by term as x2+9x^{2} + 9x2+9, dropping the −6x-6x−6x that the four products of (x−3)(x−3)(x-3)(x-3)(x−3)(x−3) supply.

    Expand both pieces first. The square owes four products, so its middle term is −6x-6x−6x, not nothing.

    (x2+3x−10)−(x2−6x+9)=x2+3x−10−x2+6x−9=9x−19(x^{2} + 3x - 10) - (x^{2} - 6x + 9) = x^{2} + 3x - 10 - x^{2} + 6x - 9 = 9x - 19(x2+3x−10)−(x2−6x+9)=x2+3x−10−x2+6x−9=9x−19

    Every term of the square changes sign: the −6x-6x−6x becomes +6x+6x+6x and the +9+9+9 becomes −9-9−9. The x2x^{2}x2 terms cancel, which is why a difference of two degree-222 expressions has come out linear.

    Advanced. This question goes beyond core Algebra I. It is not required by the course.

    The graph of y=4xy = 4^{x}y=4x passes through (2,16)(2, 16)(2,16). Which point must lie on the graph of y=log⁡4(x)y = \log_{4}(x)y=log4​(x), and what is that graph's domain?

    Answer choices for question 15

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Reflects nothing, keeping the exponential's point and its domain, though the mirror across y=xy = xy=x swaps both the coordinates and the domain with the range.

    You chose C: Swaps the coordinates but keeps the exponential's domain, though after the reflection "all real numbers" describes the logarithm's outputs, not its inputs.

    You chose D: Reads an inverse function as a reciprocal, turning each coordinate into one over itself instead of trading their places.

    A logarithm is an exponent, so the fact 42=164^{2} = 1642=16 can be read either way round.

    42=16  ⟺  log⁡4(16)=24^{2} = 16 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \log_{4}(16) = 242=16⟺log4​(16)=2

    The reflection across y=xy = xy=x swaps the coordinates of every point, so (2,16)(2, 16)(2,16) becomes (16,2)(16, 2)(16,2). It swaps the domain and the range too: the exponential accepts every real number and returns only positives, so the logarithm accepts only positives and returns every real number.

  16. 16

    As xxx runs further and further to the left, what value do the outputs of f(x)=2x+5f(x) = 2^{x} + 5f(x)=2x+5 creep toward, and what is the range of fff?

    Answer choices for question 16

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Reports the behaviour of 2x2^{x}2x on its own and never accounts for the 555 that has been added to every one of its outputs.

    You chose B: Reads a leftward run as a fall through every value, though 2x2^{x}2x stays positive no matter how negative the input becomes.

    You chose D: Includes the limiting value in the range, though 2x2^{x}2x is never exactly 000, so 2x+52^{x} + 52x+5 is never exactly 555.

    Work from 2x2^{x}2x first. It is positive at every input, and running left makes it small: 2−3=182^{-3} = \tfrac{1}{8}2−3=81​, 2−10=110242^{-10} = \tfrac{1}{1024}2−10=10241​, and the values keep shrinking toward 000 without ever arriving.

    2x>0  ⟹  2x+5>52^{x} > 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; 2^{x} + 5 > 52x>0⟹2x+5>5

    Every output of fff is exactly 555 more than the matching output of 2x2^{x}2x, so as 2x2^{x}2x creeps toward 000 the sum creeps toward 555 from above. No input makes 2x2^{x}2x equal to 000, so no output of fff equals 555, and the range is y>5y > 5y>5.

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose D: Divides the doubling factor by the growth factor, as though an exponent could be freed by ordinary division.

    P(1.06)t=2P  ⇒  (1.06)t=2  ⇒  tlog⁡(1.06)=log⁡(2)  ⇒  t=log⁡(2)log⁡(1.06)P(1.06)^{t} = 2P \;\Rightarrow\; (1.06)^{t} = 2 \;\Rightarrow\; t\log(1.06) = \log(2) \;\Rightarrow\; t = \frac{\log(2)}{\log(1.06)}P(1.06)t=2P⇒(1.06)t=2⇒tlog(1.06)=log(2)⇒t=log(1.06)log(2)​

    For which real numbers xxx is the statement log⁡ ⁣(x2)=2log⁡(x)\log\!\left(x^{2}\right) = 2\log(x)log(x2)=2log(x) true?

    Solution

    The polynomial PPP has degree 444 with leading coefficient −3-3−3, and the polynomial QQQ has degree 666 with leading coefficient 12\tfrac{1}{2}21​. What can be said about the degree of P⋅QP\cdot QP⋅Q and about the degree of P+QP + QP+Q?

    Answer choices for question 19

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Exchanges the two rules, multiplying the degrees for a product and adding them for a sum.

    You chose C: Carries the cancellation exception to a sum whose two degrees are different, where the higher leading term has no term at its own power to cancel against.

    You chose D: Takes the degree of a sum to be the sum of the two degrees, which is the rule for a product.

    The two operations behave differently, and the difference decides the second half of this question. A product multiplies the leading terms:

    (−3x4)(12x6)=−32x10\left(-3x^{4}\right)\left(\tfrac{1}{2}x^{6}\right) = -\tfrac{3}{2}x^{10}(−3x4)(21​x6)=−23​x10

    No other pair of terms reaches degree 101010, and −3×12-3 \times \tfrac{1}{2}−3×21​ is not zero, so that term survives and P⋅QP\cdot QP⋅Q has degree 101010. For the sum, cancellation needs two terms at the same power. Here PPP has no x6x^{6}x6 term at all, so QQQ's 12x6\tfrac{1}{2}x^{6}21​x6 has nothing to cancel against and P+QP + QP+Q has degree 666 outright. The cancellation warning applies only when the two polynomials share a degree.

    An exponential function f(x)=a⋅bxf(x) = a\cdot b^{x}f(x)=a⋅bx with a>0a > 0a>0, b>0b > 0b>0 and b≠1b \ne 1b=1 satisfies f(1)=12f(1) = 12f(1)=12 and f(4)=96f(4) = 96f(4)=96. What is aaa?

    Answer choices for question 20

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    11 pts

    Let P=4x3−x2+6x−2P = 4x^{3} - x^{2} + 6x - 2P=4x3−x2+6x−2 and Q=4x3+5x2−6xQ = 4x^{3} + 5x^{2} - 6xQ=4x3+5x2−6x. Write every answer in standard form, with the powers descending.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Compute P+QP + QP+Q, and state the degree of the result.

      Write the expression An equation or an expression is enough here. Show how you built it. 3 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Compute P−QP - QP−Q, and state the degree of the result.

      Write the expression An equation or an expression is enough here. Show how you built it. 4 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      Compare the degrees of your answers to parts A and B. Explain what feature of PPP and QQQ decides whether a difference can come out with a lower degree than either polynomial it was built from, and state that condition in general.

      Carry your own answer forward Compare whichever two results you produced in parts A and B, even if they were not the expected ones, and argue from what you actually obtained. The credit here is for the account of when a leading term can vanish, not for a particular pair of polynomials.

      Justify your claim State the claim, then give the reason it has to be true. 4 points

    The answer

    Part A

    P+Q=8x3+4x2−2P + Q = 8x^{3} + 4x^{2} - 2P+Q=8x3+4x2−2, of degree 333.

    • 8x3+4x2+0x−28x^{3} + 4x^{2} + 0x - 28x3+4x2+0x−2 is the same polynomial with the empty column written in; a term whose coefficient is 000 contributes nothing and is normally left out

    Part B

    P−Q=−6x2+12x−2P - Q = -6x^{2} + 12x - 2P−Q=−6x2+12x−2, of degree 222.

    • −2+12x−6x2-2 + 12x - 6x^{2}−2+12x−6x2 is the same polynomial out of order; standard form puts the highest power first, which is where the degree is read

    Part C

    The sum keeps degree 333: the leading coefficients 444 and 444 add to 888, which is not zero. The difference loses it: they subtract to 000. In general the degree can fall below both only when the two polynomials share a degree and the coefficients at that power cancel; otherwise it is the larger of the two.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    A plus sign in front of a parenthesis changes nothing inside it, so both sets of parentheses drop and every sign stays as it stands. Gather the like powers into columns.

    (4x3+4x3)+(−x2+5x2)+(6x−6x)−2=8x3+4x2−2\left(4x^{3} + 4x^{3}\right) + \left(-x^{2} + 5x^{2}\right) + \left(6x - 6x\right) - 2 = 8x^{3} + 4x^{2} - 2(4x3+4x3)+(−x2+5x2)+(6x−6x)−2=8x3+4x2−2

    The xxx column comes out empty, since 6−6=06 - 6 = 06−6=0, so no xxx term appears in the answer. The highest power present is x3x^{3}x3, so the degree is 333.

    Part B

    The minus sign in front of QQQ is a factor of −1-1−1 on the whole group, so all three of its signs turn over.

    4x3−x2+6x−2−4x3−5x2+6x=−6x2+12x−24x^{3} - x^{2} + 6x - 2 - 4x^{3} - 5x^{2} + 6x = -6x^{2} + 12x - 24x3−x2+6x−2−4x3−5x2+6x=−6x2+12x−2

    Watch the two signs that changed: the +5x2+5x^{2}+5x2 became −5x2-5x^{2}−5x2 and the −6x-6x−6x became +6x+6x+6x. The two x3x^{3}x3 terms are now equal and opposite, so they wipe each other out, and the highest power left is x2x^{2}x2: the degree is 222.

    Part C

    Both PPP and QQQ have degree 333, and both carry the identical leading term 4x34x^{3}4x3. That coincidence is what the whole question turns on, because the two operations do different things to it.

    4+4=8≠0,4−4=04 + 4 = 8 \ne 0, \qquad 4 - 4 = 04+4=8=0,4−4=0

    Adding puts 8x38x^{3}8x3 at the front, so the sum keeps degree 333. Subtracting puts 0x30x^{3}0x3 there, so that power disappears entirely and the degree drops to 222, lower than either polynomial started with.

    In general, the degree of a sum or difference is at most the larger of the two degrees, and it equals that larger degree unless the two polynomials share it and the coefficients at that power cancel. When the degrees are different, nothing can happen to the higher one at all, because the other polynomial has no term at that power to combine with it.

    In one line

    P+Q=8x3+4x2−2P + Q = 8x^{3} + 4x^{2} - 2P+Q=8x3+4x2−2, of degree 333, and P−Q=−6x2+12x−2P - Q = -6x^{2} + 12x - 2P−Q=−6x2+12x−2, of degree 222. Both polynomials carry the leading term 4x34x^{3}4x3, and 4+4=84 + 4 = 84+4=8 keeps it in the sum while 4−4=04 - 4 = 04−4=0 wipes it out of the difference. A sum or difference can fall below both original degrees only when the two polynomials share a degree and the coefficients at that power cancel; otherwise the degree is the larger of the two.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Every logarithm asks one question: the base to what power gives the input? Answer it by writing each one in exponential form.

    26=64,70=1,5−2=152=1252^{6} = 64, \qquad 7^{0} = 1, \qquad 5^{-2} = \frac{1}{5^{2}} = \frac{1}{25}26=64,70=1,5−2=521​=251​

    Write the input using only the numbers whose logarithms you were handed.

    40=8×5=23⋅540 = 8 \times 5 = 2^{3}\cdot 540=8×5=23⋅5

    Now take log⁡b\log_{b}logb​ of both sides. The product law splits the two factors into a sum, and the power law pulls the exponent 333 down in front:

    log⁡b(40)=log⁡b ⁣(23)+log⁡b(5)=3log⁡b(2)+log⁡b(5)=3(0.36)+0.83=1.91\log_{b}(40) = \log_{b}\!\left(2^{3}\right) + \log_{b}(5) = 3\log_{b}(2) + \log_{b}(5) = 3(0.36) + 0.83 = 1.91logb​(40)=logb​(23)+logb​(5)=3logb​(2)+logb​(5)=3(0.36)+0.83=1.91

    The line is false. The law it is reaching for is the product law,

    log⁡b(MN)=log⁡b(M)+log⁡b(N),\log_{b}(MN) = \log_{b}(M) + \log_{b}(N),logb​(MN)=logb​(M)+logb​(N),

    and what that law requires of its two inputs is that they be MULTIPLIED, not added. Here 2×5=102 \times 5 = 102×5=10, so the right-hand side is the logarithm of 101010:

    and log⁡b(7)\log_{b}(7)logb​(7) is a different number, because a logarithm is one-to-one and 7≠107 \ne 107=10. A small case makes the same point with numbers you can check by hand: with base 222, log⁡2(4+4)=log⁡2(8)=3\log_{2}(4 + 4) = \log_{2}(8) = 3log2​(4+4)=log2​(8)=3, while log⁡2(4)+log⁡2(4)=2+2=4\log_{2}(4) + \log_{2}(4) = 2 + 2 = 4log2​(4)+log2​(4)=2+2=4. The line log⁡b(7)=log⁡b(2)+log⁡b(5)\log_{b}(7) = \log_{b}(2) + \log_{b}(5)logb​(7)=logb​(2)+logb​(5) is false: the product law adds logarithms when the inputs are multiplied, so that sum is log⁡b(10)=1.19\log_{b}(10) = 1.19logb​(10)=1.19, and there is no law for the logarithm of a sum.

      Part C.

      Parts A and B each asked you to form every product of a term from the first factor with a term from the second. State the rule that decides how many such products a multiplication owes before any like terms are collected. Then explain why the degree of a product can never come out lower than the degree of either factor.

      Carry your own answer forward Count the products in whichever expansions you actually carried out in parts A and B. The credit here is for the counting rule and for the argument about the leading terms, not for the two particular answers.

    The answer

    Part A

    6x2+7x−206x^{2} + 7x - 206x2+7x−20.

    • 6x2+15x−8x−206x^{2} + 15x - 8x - 206x2+15x−8x−20 is the same expression with the like terms not yet collected; standard form gathers them into 7x7x7x

    Part B

    3x3+5x2+4x+123x^{3} + 5x^{2} + 4x + 123x3+5x2+4x+12.

    • 3x3−x2+6x+6x2−2x+123x^{3} - x^{2} + 6x + 6x^{2} - 2x + 123x3−x2+6x+6x2−2x+12 is the same expression with the six products not yet gathered; standard form combines them

    Part C

    A factor with ppp terms times a factor with qqq terms owes pqpqpq products: 444 in part A and 666 in part B. The degree cannot drop because the two leading terms multiply into a single term whose degree is the sum of the two factors' degrees; no other pairing reaches that power, and two nonzero coefficients cannot multiply to zero.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Two terms times two terms owes four products, and every sign travels with its own term.

    (3x)(2x)+(3x)(5)+(−4)(2x)+(−4)(5)=6x2+15x−8x−20(3x)(2x) + (3x)(5) + (-4)(2x) + (-4)(5) = 6x^{2} + 15x - 8x - 20(3x)(2x)+(3x)(5)+(−4)(2x)+(−4)(5)=6x2+15x−8x−20

    The two middle products carry the same power of xxx, so they combine to 7x7x7x, and the answer is 6x2+7x−206x^{2} + 7x - 206x2+7x−20.

    Part B

    Two terms times three terms owes 2×3=62 \times 3 = 62×3=6 products, so the four-product pattern is not enough here. Distribute xxx across the trinomial, then 222 across it.

    x(3x2−x+6)=3x3−x2+6x,2(3x2−x+6)=6x2−2x+12x\left(3x^{2} - x + 6\right) = 3x^{3} - x^{2} + 6x, \qquad 2\left(3x^{2} - x + 6\right) = 6x^{2} - 2x + 12x(3x2−x+6)=3x3−x2+6x,2(3x2−x+6)=6x2−2x+12

    Add the two rows and gather like powers: −x2+6x2=5x2-x^{2} + 6x^{2} = 5x^{2}−x2+6x2=5x2 and 6x−2x=4x6x - 2x = 4x6x−2x=4x, so the product is 3x3+5x2+4x+123x^{3} + 5x^{2} + 4x + 123x3+5x2+4x+12.

    Part C

    How many products. A factor with mmm terms times a factor with nnn terms produces m×nm \times nm×n products, one for each pairing, before anything is collected. Part A was 2×2=42 \times 2 = 42×2=4 and part B was 2×3=62 \times 3 = 62×3=6. That is exactly why the four-product mnemonic describes a binomial times a binomial and nothing wider.

    Why the degree cannot drop. Write each factor in standard form, so its first term is its leading term, say axma x^{m}axm and bxnb x^{n}bxn. Multiply those two:

    (axm)(bxn)=ab xm+n.\left(a x^{m}\right)\left(b x^{n}\right) = ab\,x^{m+n}.(axm)(bxn)=abxm+n.

    Every other product pairs a term of degree at most mmm with a term of degree at most nnn, and in each such pairing at least one factor has a strictly smaller degree, so every other product has degree strictly less than m+nm + nm+n. That leaves ab xm+nab\,x^{m+n}abxm+n alone at its power with nothing to combine with, and ab≠0ab \ne 0ab=0 because neither leading coefficient is zero. So the top term survives and the degree is m+nm + nm+n, which is at least mmm and at least nnn.

    A sum behaves differently for one reason only: there the two leading terms can land in the same column and be ADDED, and two nonzero numbers can add to zero. In a product they are multiplied, and nonzero times nonzero is never zero.

    In one line

    (3x−4)(2x+5)=6x2+7x−20(3x - 4)(2x + 5) = 6x^{2} + 7x - 20(3x−4)(2x+5)=6x2+7x−20 and (x+2)(3x2−x+6)=3x3+5x2+4x+12(x + 2)\left(3x^{2} - x + 6\right) = 3x^{3} + 5x^{2} + 4x + 12(x+2)(3x2−x+6)=3x3+5x2+4x+12. A factor with ppp terms times a factor with qqq terms owes pqpqpq products, which is 444 and then 666 here. The degree of a product is always the sum of the two factors' degrees: the leading terms multiply into a single term at that power, no other pairing reaches it, and a product of two nonzero coefficients is nonzero, so it cannot be cancelled. A sum can lose its top term only because addition, unlike multiplication, can turn two nonzero numbers into zero.

    It cannot. For every real xxx, 0.6x0.6^{x}0.6x is a positive base raised to a real power and so is positive, and 777 is positive, so every output is a positive times a positive.     Part A

    A positive multiplier times a positive base raised to any real power is positive, so every output is positive and the range is y>0y > 0y>0.     Part C

    It never happens, and the reason is in the rule rather than in any table of values. A positive base raised to a real power is positive: a whole-number exponent multiplies positive numbers together, a negative exponent takes the reciprocal of a positive number, and a fractional exponent takes a root of a positive number.

    The answer

    Part A

    A+B=x2+4x−4A + B = x^{2} + 4x - 4A+B=x2+4x−4, of degree 222.

    • 0x3+x2+4x−40x^{3} + x^{2} + 4x - 40x3+x2+4x−4 is the same polynomial with the empty column written in; a term whose coefficient is 000 contributes nothing and is normally left out

    Part B

    A⋅BA\cdot BA⋅B has degree 666, with leading term −4x6-4x^{6}−4x6.

    Part C

    The product rule always holds: the leading terms multiply, and two nonzero coefficients cannot multiply to zero. The sum rule can fail, and part A is a counterexample: 2x32x^{3}2x3 and −2x3-2x^{3}−2x3 added to zero, dropping the degree from 333 to 222. Addition can cancel a leading coefficient; multiplication cannot.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Adding changes no signs, so both sets of parentheses drop and the like powers are gathered as they stand.

    (2x3−2x3)+x2+4x+(−5+1)=x2+4x−4\left(2x^{3} - 2x^{3}\right) + x^{2} + 4x + (-5 + 1) = x^{2} + 4x - 4(2x3−2x3)+x2+4x+(−5+1)=x2+4x−4

    The two leading coefficients are 222 and −2-2−2, which add to 000, so the x3x^{3}x3 column empties and the highest power left is x2x^{2}x2. The degree is 222.

    Part B

    Only the two leading terms can reach the top power, so the front of the product is settled without touching the other eight products.

    (2x3)(−2x3)=−4x6\left(2x^{3}\right)\left(-2x^{3}\right) = -4x^{6}(2x3)(−2x3)=−4x6

    Every other pairing multiplies a term of degree at most 333 by a term of degree at most 333 with at least one of them strictly smaller, so no other product reaches degree 666. Since −4-4−4 is not zero, that term survives with nothing at its power to cancel it, and the degree is 3+3=63 + 3 = 63+3=6.

    Part C

    The product rule holds without exception. The leading terms of AAA and BBB are multiplied, not added, and their coefficients are 222 and −2-2−2:

    2×(−2)=−4≠0.2 \times (-2) = -4 \ne 0.2×(−2)=−4=0.

    A product of two nonzero numbers is never zero, and no other pairing of terms reaches degree 666, so the top term of A⋅BA\cdot BA⋅B always survives. That is why the degree of a product is the sum of the degrees, with no exceptions.

    The sum rule can fail, and part A shows it failing. There the same two leading coefficients meet under addition instead:

    2+(−2)=0,2 + (-2) = 0,2+(−2)=0,

    so the x3x^{3}x3 term disappears and A+BA + BA+B has degree 222, not the 333 the rule as stated would predict. The honest version is that the degree of a sum is at most the larger of the two degrees, and equals it unless the two polynomials share that degree and their leading coefficients cancel.

    The whole difference is which operation the two leading coefficients meet under. Addition can send two nonzero numbers to zero; multiplication cannot.

The difference is the operation the two leading coefficients meet under, since addition can send two nonzero numbers to zero and multiplication cannot.

    Three statements are in circulation:

    (1)    (a+b)2=a2+b2,(2)    log⁡(M+N)=log⁡(M)+log⁡(N),(3)    2x+y=2x+2y.(1)\;\; (a+b)^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2}, \qquad (2)\;\; \log(M + N) = \log(M) + \log(N), \qquad (3)\;\; 2^{x+y} = 2^{x} + 2^{y}.(1)(a+b)2=a2+b2,(2)log(M+N)=log(M)+log(N),(3)2x+y=2x+2y.

    Each one takes an addition inside a bracket and lets it pass straight through unchanged. Here log⁡\loglog is the common logarithm, and MMM and NNN are positive.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Show that statement (1) is false by choosing numbers for aaa and bbb and evaluating both sides. Then write down the correct expansion of (a+b)2(a + b)^{2}(a+b)2 and name the term the false version loses.

      Construct a counterexample Give one specific case, and show it breaks the claim. 4 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Do the same for statements (2) and (3): choose numbers, show that the two sides disagree, and in each case write down the true law that has that shape.

      Construct a counterexample Give one specific case, and show it breaks the claim. 4 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      State in one sentence what the three false statements have in common. Then explain, for each of the three true laws you have written down, why the operation on one side is not the operation on the other.

      Carry your own answer forward Build the summary on the counterexamples and the corrected laws you produced in parts A and B, whatever they were. The credit here is for naming the shared assumption and for saying what each true law trades, not for particular numbers.

      Explain why it works A sentence or two. Reasons, not steps. 5 points

    The answer

    Part A

    With a=2a = 2a=2 and b=3b = 3b=3: (2+3)2=25(2+3)^{2} = 25(2+3)2=25 while 22+32=132^{2} + 3^{2} = 1322+32=13. The correct expansion is (a+b)2=a2+2ab+b2(a+b)^{2} = a^{2} + 2ab + b^{2}(a+b)2=a2+2ab+b2, and the false version drops the cross term 2ab2ab2ab, which is 121212 here.

    Part B

    With M=N=10M = N = 10M=N=10: log⁡(M)+log⁡(N)=2\log(M) + \log(N) = 2log(M)+log(N)=2, which is log⁡(100)\log(100)log(100), not log⁡(20)\log(20)log(20), since log⁡(20)=2\log(20) = 2log(20)=2 would say 102=2010^{2} = 20102=20. The true law is log⁡(MN)=log⁡(M)+log⁡(N)\log(MN) = \log(M) + \log(N)log(MN)=log(M)+log(N). With x=y=3x = y = 3x=y=3: 26=642^{6} = 6426=64 but 23+23=162^{3} + 2^{3} = 1623+23=16; the true law is 2x+y=2x⋅2y2^{x+y} = 2^{x}\cdot 2^{y}2x+y=2x⋅2y.

    Part C

    All three let an addition inside a bracket pass through unchanged. Each true law trades one operation for a different one: a square of a sum owes the cross term 2ab2ab2ab; a logarithm turns multiplication into addition, not addition into addition; and an exponential turns addition in the exponent into multiplication.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Take a=2a = 2a=2 and b=3b = 3b=3 and evaluate the two sides separately.

    (2+3)2=52=25,22+32=4+9=13(2 + 3)^{2} = 5^{2} = 25, \qquad 2^{2} + 3^{2} = 4 + 9 = 13(2+3)2=52=25,22+32=4+9=13

    They are different numbers, so the statement is false. Squaring a sum means (a+b)(a+b)(a+b)(a+b)(a+b)(a+b), and every term of the first factor multiplies every term of the second, which is four products rather than two:

    (a+b)(a+b)=a2+ab+ba+b2=a2+2ab+b2.(a+b)(a+b) = a^{2} + ab + ba + b^{2} = a^{2} + 2ab + b^{2}.(a+b)(a+b)=a2+ab+ba+b2=a2+2ab+b2.

    The false version keeps the first and last products and discards the two cross terms, whose sum is 2ab2ab2ab. With these numbers that missing piece is 2(2)(3)=122(2)(3) = 122(2)(3)=12, and 13+12=2513 + 12 = 2513+12=25 closes the gap exactly.

    Part B

    Statement (2). Take M=N=10M = N = 10M=N=10, where both logarithms are known exactly.

    log⁡(10)+log⁡(10)=1+1=2,log⁡(10+10)=log⁡(20)\log(10) + \log(10) = 1 + 1 = 2, \qquad \log(10 + 10) = \log(20)log(10)+log(10)=1+1=2,log(10+10)=log(20)

    If log⁡(20)\log(20)log(20) were 222 it would say 102=2010^{2} = 20102=20, which is false, so the two sides are different and the statement fails. What the sum 222 actually is is log⁡(100)\log(100)log(100), and 100=10×10100 = 10 \times 10100=10×10: the law with this shape is the product law, log⁡(MN)=log⁡(M)+log⁡(N)\log(MN) = \log(M) + \log(N)log(MN)=log(M)+log(N), which asks for the two inputs to be MULTIPLIED. There is no law at all for the logarithm of a sum.

    Statement (3). Take x=y=3x = y = 3x=y=3.

    23+3=26=64,23+23=8+8=162^{3+3} = 2^{6} = 64, \qquad 2^{3} + 2^{3} = 8 + 8 = 1623+3=26=64,23+23=8+8=16

    Again the sides disagree. The law with this shape is 2x+y=2x⋅2y2^{x+y} = 2^{x}\cdot 2^{y}2x+y=2x⋅2y: adding to the exponent MULTIPLIES the outputs, and 8×8=648 \times 8 = 648×8=64 confirms it.

    Part C

    What they share. Each false statement assumes that an operation applied to a bracket can be handed to the terms inside it one at a time, so an addition inside comes out as an addition outside. None of the three settings works that way.

    Squaring a sum. (a+b)2(a+b)^{2}(a+b)2 is (a+b)(a+b)(a+b)(a+b)(a+b)(a+b), and every term of the first factor multiplies every term of the second, giving four products rather than two. Two of them are the cross terms ababab and bababa, so the honest identity is a2+2ab+b2a^{2} + 2ab + b^{2}a2+2ab+b2, and the middle term is precisely what the false version discards.

    A logarithm. A logarithm is an exponent, and exponents ADD when the powers are MULTIPLIED. So the law converts a product of inputs into a sum of logarithms:

    log⁡(MN)=log⁡(M)+log⁡(N).\log(MN) = \log(M) + \log(N).log(MN)=log(M)+log(N).

    The operation changes as it crosses the equals sign, which is the whole value of the law, and a sum of inputs is left with no rule at all.

    An exponential. The same exponent fact read the other way gives 2x+y=2x⋅2y2^{x+y} = 2^{x}\cdot 2^{y}2x+y=2x⋅2y: adding to the input multiplies the output. Again the operation changes, addition on the left becoming multiplication on the right.

    So in all three cases the true statement trades one operation for another, and a rule that hands the same operation straight through is the shape to distrust.

    In one line

    All three statements are false. With a=2a = 2a=2 and b=3b = 3b=3: (2+3)2=25(2+3)^{2} = 25(2+3)2=25 but 22+32=132^{2} + 3^{2} = 1322+32=13, and the true expansion a2+2ab+b2a^{2} + 2ab + b^{2}a2+2ab+b2 supplies the missing 2ab=122ab = 122ab=12. With M=N=10M = N = 10M=N=10: the sum of the logarithms is 222, which is log⁡(100)\log(100)log(100) rather than log⁡(20)\log(20)log(20), and the true law is log⁡(MN)=log⁡(M)+log⁡(N)\log(MN) = \log(M) + \log(N)log(MN)=log(M)+log(N). With x=y=3x = y = 3x=y=3: 26=642^{6} = 6426=64 but 23+23=162^{3} + 2^{3} = 1623+23=16, and the true law is 2x+y=2x⋅2y2^{x+y} = 2^{x}\cdot 2^{y}2x+y=2x⋅2y. What the three share is the assumption that an addition inside a bracket passes through unchanged, when in truth each law trades one operation for a different one.

    9. Two functions compared over several inputs . 13 points. Question 9 of 10.

    13 pts

    Let f(x)=5⋅2xf(x) = 5\cdot 2^{x}f(x)=5⋅2x and g(x)=5+30xg(x) = 5 + 30xg(x)=5+30x, both compared at the whole-number inputs x=0,1,2,3,…x = 0, 1, 2, 3, \ldotsx=0,1,2,3,….

    1. A
      Part A.

      Evaluate fff and ggg at x=0x = 0x=0, 111, 222, 333, 444 and 555, and state the value each rule gives at x=0x = 0x=0.

      Part B.

      Carry your own answer forward Use whichever values you produced in part A, even if they were not the expected ones, and report honestly where each function is the larger. The credit here is for testing the claim against your own numbers and for the claim your own numbers actually support.

      Part C.

Use that to explain how the two functions compare far to the right of the inputs you tried, and say why no single input can establish a claim made about every input, even though one input was enough to settle the claim in part B.

      Justify your claim State the claim, then give the reason it has to be true. 6 points

    The answer

    Part A

    fff gives 555, 101010, 202020, 404040, 808080, 160160160, and ggg gives 555, 353535, 656565, 959595, 125125125, 155155155. Both graphs meet the vertical axis at 555.

    Part B

    It does not hold. At x=1x = 1x=1, f(1)=10f(1) = 10f(1)=10 while g(1)=35g(1) = 35g(1)=35, so the exponential is the smaller there, and the same holds at x=2x = 2x=2, 333 and 444. What the values support is that the exponential is EVENTUALLY larger and then stays larger, which here begins at x=5x = 5x=5.

    Part C

    ggg gains a fixed 303030 each step, while fff is multiplied by 222, so fff's gain per step equals its current value and grows along with it. Once fff is ahead, its gain already exceeds 303030 and keeps rising, so it cannot be caught. One input reports one comparison, so it can refute a claim made about every input but can never establish one.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Each unit step multiplies fff by the base 222 and adds 303030 to ggg, so both rows can be built by hand.

    f:  5, 10, 20, 40, 80, 160g:  5, 35, 65, 95, 125, 155f: \; 5,\ 10,\ 20,\ 40,\ 80,\ 160 \qquad\qquad g: \; 5,\ 35,\ 65,\ 95,\ 125,\ 155f:5, 10, 20, 40, 80, 160g:5, 35, 65, 95, 125, 155

    The vertical intercept of each is its value at x=0x = 0x=0. For the exponential, f(0)=5⋅20=5×1=5f(0) = 5\cdot 2^{0} = 5\times 1 = 5f(0)=5⋅20=5×1=5, because any allowed base to the zero power is 111; for the line, g(0)=5+30(0)=5g(0) = 5 + 30(0) = 5g(0)=5+30(0)=5. Both begin at 555.

    Part B

    The claim fails immediately. Compare the two rows at x=1x = 1x=1:

    f(1)=10againstg(1)=35f(1) = 10 \qquad \text{against} \qquad g(1) = 35f(1)=10againstg(1)=35

    The linear function is the larger there, and again at x=2x = 2x=2 (202020 against 656565), at x=3x = 3x=3 (404040 against 959595) and at x=4x = 4x=4 (808080 against 125125125). A single input where the exponential is smaller is enough to sink a claim that says "always".

    What the values do support is a claim with a timing word in it. At x=5x = 5x=5 the order changes, 160160160 against 155155155, and from there the exponential is ahead. So the honest statement is that an exponential with base greater than 111 eventually exceeds a linear function and then stays above it, not that it is larger at every input.

    Part C

    Look at what one unit step does to each rule, rather than at the numbers the rules produce.

    g(x+1)−g(x)=30,f(x+1)−f(x)=5⋅2x+1−5⋅2x=5⋅2x=f(x)g(x+1) - g(x) = 30, \qquad f(x+1) - f(x) = 5\cdot 2^{x+1} - 5\cdot 2^{x} = 5\cdot 2^{x} = f(x)g(x+1)−g(x)=30,f(x+1)−f(x)=5⋅2x+1−5⋅2x=5⋅2x=f(x)

    The linear function gains the same fixed 303030 at every step, however large it has grown. The exponential gains its own current value, so its step gain grows in proportion to the function itself. A fixed gain cannot keep pace with a growing one indefinitely, which is why the exponential must overtake.

    Staying ahead follows from the same two lines. Suppose f(x)>g(x)f(x) > g(x)f(x)>g(x) at some input with x≥1x \ge 1x≥1. Then f(x)>g(x)≥35>30f(x) > g(x) \ge 35 > 30f(x)>g(x)≥35>30, so at the next step fff gains more than ggg does and the lead widens instead of closing, and every further step makes fff's gain larger still.

    A single input can never settle a claim of this kind, because it reports one comparison and nothing else. Testing x=1x = 1x=1 here would report that the linear function is larger and testing x=5x = 5x=5 would report the opposite, and neither on its own describes what happens across all inputs.

The claim that an exponential with base greater than 111 is always larger is false: at x=1,2,3x = 1, 2, 3x=1,2,3 and 444 the linear function is the larger of the two. The corrected claim is that the exponential is eventually larger and then stays larger, which here begins at x=5x = 5x=5. The reason is in the per-step change: ggg gains a fixed 303030 every step while fff gains its own current value, so once fff is ahead its gain already exceeds 303030 and keeps growing.

As nnn grows, the inner bracket rises by smaller and smaller amounts toward ere^{r}er, because (1+1m)m\left(1 + \tfrac{1}{m}\right)^{m}(1+m1​)m crowds toward e≈2.71828e \approx 2.71828e≈2.71828. Part B 4

  • Distributes the minus sign to every term of the second polynomial, not to the first one only. 2
  • Combines the like terms correctly and writes the result in descending order. 1
  • Names the degree from the highest power that actually survives, not from the polynomials it came from. 1

Part C 4

  • Locates the cause in the two leading coefficients, showing that one combination is zero and the other is not, rather than quoting a rule. 3
  • States the general condition with both of its halves: the same degree, and coefficients at that power that cancel. 1

2. Exponents read off, and three of them put together 12 points

Part A 3

  • Rewrites each logarithm as the exponential statement it stands for, rather than reaching for a formula. 2
  • Reports each answer as the exponent itself, including the negative value for the reciprocal input. 1

Part B 5

  • Factors the input into powers of the numbers whose logarithms are given, instead of looking for a rule that acts on 404040 directly. 2
  • Applies the product law to the two factors and the power law to the exponent, then substitutes the given values. 2
  • Reports a single number as the value of the logarithm. 1

Part C 4

  • Reaches a verdict and grounds it in what the product law actually asks of its two inputs, rather than in the line looking unfamiliar. 3
  • Backs the verdict with a computation, either the given values or a small case checked by hand. 1

3. Every term meeting every term, twice over 12 points

Part A 3

  • Forms all four products, carrying each sign into the product it belongs to. 2
  • Collects the two like middle terms and reports the result in descending order. 1

Part B 4

  • Multiplies every term of the binomial by every term of the trinomial, six products in all rather than four. 2
  • Combines the like powers correctly and reports the result in descending order. 2

Part C 5

  • States the counting rule as the product of the two term counts and matches it against both expansions. 1
  • Argues that the two leading terms multiply into a single top-degree term that no other pairing reaches, and that its coefficient cannot be zero. 3
  • Runs the argument in general letters, so it covers any two polynomials rather than only the two expanded above. 1

4. Four outputs, and the curve they belong to 13 points

Part A 4

  • Tests the ratios between consecutive outputs, using that the inputs are equally spaced rather than assuming it. 2
  • Takes the base from the constant ratio and the multiplier from the output at x=0x = 0x=0, and writes the rule out. 2

Part B 5

  • Decides the direction from where the base sits relative to 111, not from the look of the listed numbers. 2
  • Evaluates the rule at x=0x = 0x=0 to get the vertical intercept. 1
  • States the range and the value the outputs creep toward, and keeps the two consistent with each other. 2

Part C 4

  • Argues from a positive base raised to a real power always being positive, rather than from the outputs merely looking small. 3
  • Describes what the outputs do instead, in terms of the horizontal asymptote, consistently with the sign argument. 1

5. One rate, three schedules 13 points

Part A 4

  • Writes the rate as a decimal and, for the quarterly schedule, divides it by 444 while multiplying the exponent by 444. 2
  • Carries out both calculations and rounds only the final balances, not the growth factors. 1
  • States both answers as amounts of money to the nearest cent. 1

Part B 4

  • Uses A=PertA = Pe^{rt}A=Pert with the product of rate and time in the exponent, not the rate alone. 2
  • Computes the balance and then the gap against the earlier figure. 1
  • Reports both the balance and the gap as amounts of money. 1

Part C 5

  • Orders the three balances and observes that the gains between them are shrinking, not merely that they are positive. 2
  • Ties the ceiling to the factor for one year approaching ere^{r}er, rather than asserting without reason that the balance is bounded. 2
  • Names the continuous formula as the ceiling itself, so the limit is a specific amount rather than a vague bound. 1

6. Two operations, two rules about degree 12 points

Part A 3

  • Adds coefficients within each power and leaves the powers themselves untouched. 2
  • Names the degree from the highest power that actually survives the addition. 1

Part B 4

  • Works from the two leading terms alone and says why the other products cannot reach that power. 2
  • Multiplies the leading coefficients and adds the exponents, reporting both the degree and the whole leading term. 2

Part C 5

  • Reaches a separate verdict on each of the two rules rather than one verdict covering both. 2
  • Supports whichever rule fails with an instance from the student's own work, identifying the coefficients responsible. 2
  • Names the operation the two leading coefficients meet under as what makes the two cases differ. 1

7. A balance run forward, and a question that runs it backward 13 points

Part A 4

  • Uses the decimal rate and an exponent equal to the number of years, with the principal outside the power. 2
  • Multiplies through and rounds only the final balance. 1
  • States the answer as an amount of money to the nearest cent. 1

Part B 5

  • Sets the balance equal to twice the principal and cancels it, rather than picking a particular deposit to work with. 1
  • Takes a logarithm of both sides and uses the power law to bring the exponent down. 2
  • Divides to reach a quotient of two logarithms and evaluates it to one decimal place. 1
  • Answers the second question, saying what the cancellation of the principal means for deposits of other sizes. 1

Part C 4

  • Compares the ten-year balance against twice the deposit and uses the doubling time to account for the gap, rather than reporting the two answers side by side. 2
  • Decides the quarterly case from how the growth of the balance changes, not by guessing a direction. 2

8. One tempting move, appearing in three places 13 points

Part A 4

  • Chooses specific numbers and evaluates both sides, so that two values can actually be compared. 2
  • Gives the correct expansion with the cross term present. 1
  • Names the dropped term and matches its value against the gap between the two sides. 1

Part B 4

  • Produces a numerical counterexample for each of the two statements, with both sides evaluated or exactly accounted for. 2
  • States the true law behind each shape, with the correct operation on each side of it. 2

Part C 5

  • Names the shared assumption as an operation being handed unchanged to the terms inside a bracket, rather than listing the three statements again. 2
  • Says, for each true law, which operation stands on each side and why the two differ. 3

9. Two functions compared over several inputs 13 points

Part A 3

  • Evaluates both rules at all six inputs, multiplying by the base for one and adding a fixed amount for the other. 2
  • Reads each vertical intercept as the value at x=0x = 0x=0, using that a base raised to the zero power is 111 rather than 000. 1

Part B 4

  • Settles the claim by exhibiting a specific input and quoting both values there, rather than asserting a verdict. 2
  • States the claim the values support, carrying a timing word, and identifies where in the values the order changes. 2

Part C 6

  • Argues from the per-step change of each rule, a fixed addition set against a multiplication, rather than from the size of the listed values. 3
  • Accounts for the lead being permanent once it is taken, not only for the overtaking happening at all. 2
  • Says why one input can refute a claim made about every input but can never establish one. 1

10. One rate, two schedules, and a limit neither can pass 16 points

Part A 5

  • Computes the ten-year value using the decimal rate and one growth factor per year. 2
  • Sets the balance equal to twice the principal, takes a logarithm of both sides, and reaches a quotient of two logarithms. 2
  • Reports the value as an amount of money and the doubling time as a number of years. 1

Part B 5

  • Divides the rate by 444 and counts 4t4t4t periods, so the exponent solved for is a period count. 2
  • Solves for the period count and converts it back into years before making any comparison. 2
  • States the gap between the two doubling times, in years. 1

Part C 6

  • Identifies the limiting case as continuous compounding and ties it to the one-year factor climbing toward ere^{r}er, rather than asserting a bound. 3
  • Solves the continuous doubling condition, using the natural logarithm because the base is eee. 2
  • Places the two earlier doubling times against the limit and notes that each rise in frequency buys less than the rise before it. 1
